Shaffer & Ginsberg, Front Public Health 2017 — heart rate metrics and norms

nodes.title: Heart rate variability from a wearable
nodes.summary: Beat-to-beat interval variation, usually reported as overnight RMSSD — the most over-interpreted number in consumer health.

attrs.what_it_estimates: Parasympathetic activity during measurement. Loosely related to recovery and training load; not a measure of aerobic fitness and not a health score.
attrs.between_person_uselessness: Between-person comparison is meaningless — normal RMSSD spans roughly an order of magnitude across healthy adults, and it falls steeply with age. Comparing your number to a friend's tells you nothing.
attrs.within_person_value: Only interpretable as a personal deviation from a personal rolling baseline, and even then day-to-day variation is large enough that single-day changes are usually noise.
attrs.measurement_dependence: Values depend on measurement window, posture, breathing rate, device and the manufacturer's algorithm — the same night processed two ways gives two numbers.
attrs.why_it_is_here: It is the marker users most want to act on and the one where a Tier C label does the most work.

citations: Shaffer & Ginsberg, Front Public Health 2017 — an overview of heart rate variability metrics and norms
Plews et al. Sports Med 2013 — heart rate variability training monitoring in athletes
Task Force of ESC and NASPE, Circulation 1996 — HRV standards of measurement

nodes.title: Daily step count
nodes.summary: Steps counted by a phone or wrist device — the most-collected health datum in existence and a reasonable proxy for total activity volume.

attrs.what_it_estimates: Ambulatory activity volume. Not intensity, and not cardiorespiratory fitness.
attrs.device_disagreement: Wrist and hip devices disagree by 10 percent or more, and phones miss everything done without the phone. Cross-device comparison is not valid.
attrs.dose_evidence: Mortality benefit rises steeply from about 2,500 to 7,500 steps per day and plateaus after roughly 8,000–10,000 depending on age — the 10,000 figure originated in 1960s marketing, not evidence.
attrs.what_it_misses: Cycling, swimming and rowing register as almost nothing, which will make a well-trained cyclist look sedentary.

citations: Paluch et al. Lancet Public Health 2022 — daily steps and all-cause mortality meta-analysis
Lee et al. JAMA Intern Med 2019 — steps per day and mortality in older women
Bassett et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2017 — step counting accuracy across devices

nodes.title: Sleep duration from a wearable
nodes.summary: Total sleep time estimated from movement and heart rate — good at total duration, considerably weaker at anything finer.

attrs.what_it_estimates: Total sleep time and, much less reliably, sleep stage composition.
attrs.what_it_is_good_at: Total sleep duration in healthy sleepers, where consumer devices agree reasonably with polysomnography.
attrs.what_it_is_bad_at: Stage classification, and detecting wake after sleep onset. Devices systematically overestimate sleep in people who sleep badly — precisely the people who want to know.
attrs.exposure_not_function: Included as an exposure proxy rather than a direct measure of any metabolic function. It tells you whether the sleep-duration intervention is actually happening; it does not measure insulin sensitivity. The graph labels the link weak for exactly this reason.
attrs.reference_standard: Polysomnography, which belongs to the sleep component rather than this one.

citations: de Zambotti et al. Sleep 2019 — validation of consumer sleep-tracking devices
Chinoy et al. Sleep 2021 — performance of seven consumer sleep-tracking devices against polysomnography
Watson et al. Sleep 2015 — AASM/SRS consensus on sleep duration

nodes.title: Session rating of perceived exertion
nodes.summary: How hard the session felt, on a 0–10 scale, recorded shortly after finishing — subjective, free, and better at tracking training load than most people expect.

attrs.what_it_estimates: Internal training load. Multiplied by duration it gives a session load that tracks reasonably with heart-rate-derived load in trained people.
attrs.why_a_tier_D_marker_earns_its_place: It works when the heart rate signal does not — swimming, heavy strength work, hot conditions, or a dead battery. A self-report that is always available beats a sensor value that is often missing.
attrs.known_biases: Anchored to the individual's experience, drifts with mood and expectation, and is systematically compressed by people who have never trained hard.
attrs.scale_discipline: Only meaningful if the same anchored scale is used every time; a scale re-explained differently is a new instrument.

citations: Borg G. Med Sci Sports Exerc 1982 — psychophysical bases of perceived exertion
Foster et al. J Strength Cond Res 2001 — session RPE method for monitoring training load
Haddad et al. Front Neurosci 2017 — session-RPE validity and influencing factors

nodes.title: Self-reported dietary intake
nodes.summary: What the user says they ate — food logs, recalls and questionnaires. The only practical way to know about diet, and the least accurate measurement in the graph.

attrs.what_it_estimates: Energy, macronutrient and fibre intake, with substantial and non-random error.
attrs.the_size_of_the_error: Energy intake is under-reported by roughly 20–30 percent on average against doubly-labelled water, and the under-reporting is worse in people with higher body weight — so the error is systematic, not just noisy.
attrs.reactivity: The act of logging changes what people eat, which is useful as an intervention and corrupting as a measurement.
attrs.honest_use: Good for tracking a specific tracked thing — protein grams, fibre grams, alcohol units — and poor for total energy. Do not compute an energy deficit from it and treat the result as a number.
attrs.why_it_stays: Every nutrition intervention in this graph is invisible without it. The right response is to label it Tier D loudly, not to pretend a better instrument exists outside a metabolic ward.

citations: Subar et al. Am J Epidemiol 2015 — addressing current criticism of dietary assessment methodology
Schoeller DA. Metabolism 1995 — limitations in the assessment of dietary energy intake by self-report
Freedman et al. Am J Epidemiol 2014 — biomarker-based validation of self-reported intake

attrs.dose: Start walking within about 15–30 minutes of finishing the meal. Two to five minutes measurably blunts the excursion; 10–20 minutes at an easy pace does more. attrs.mechanism: Contracting muscle translocates GLUT4 independently of insulin, so glucose is taken up during the absorptive window rather than after it.
attrs.magnitude: Meta-analysed reductions in postprandial glucose area under the curve are consistent across trials and clinically visible on a CGM trace — typically a substantially lower and earlier-resolving peak.
attrs.evidence_ceiling: Rated moderate rather than high because the outcome measured is a same-day surrogate. No trial has shown that habitual post-meal walking prevents diabetes or cardiovascular events over and above the effect of the activity volume it adds.
attrs.certainty_reasoning: Certainty is rated high even though evidence is moderate: the acute effect is highly reproducible and mechanistically obvious. The uncertainty is about long-run consequence, not about whether the glucose curve moves.

attrs.dose: 3–4 sessions per week of 45–60 minutes at conversational pace, progressing weekly volume by no more than about 10 percent. Expect measurable VO2max change in 6–12 weeks and continued gains over a year or more in a previously untrained person.
attrs.magnitude: Untrained adults typically gain 10–20 percent in VO2max over three to six months of consistent moderate aerobic training; trained people gain far less and need intensity work to move at all.
attrs.attia_position: Attia prescribes roughly 3–4 hours per week of Zone 2 as the aerobic foundation — about double the guideline minimum of 150 minutes of moderate activity.
attrs.consensus_note: The effect of this training on aerobic capacity is not in dispute and is rated high. attrs.risk_reasoning: Risk is rated moderate, not low, because running injury incidence in recreational runners is substantial and concentrated in the first months. The graph refuses to hide the main reason this intervention fails.
attrs.reversibility_note: Detraining is fast — meaningful VO2max loss within two to four weeks of stopping. The gain is rented, not owned.

attrs.dose: Blocks of 45 minutes or more are conventionally recommended on the argument that mitochondrial signalling responds to sustained duration; total weekly volume of 3–4 hours. attrs.mechanism: Endurance training increases mitochondrial density, oxidative enzyme activity and fat oxidation capacity, and improves lactate clearance.
attrs.attia_position: Attia treats Zone 2 as specifically and near-uniquely the driver of mitochondrial function and metabolic flexibility, with the 45-minute block length as a meaningful threshold.
attrs.consensus_note: That endurance training builds mitochondria is settled physiology from the 1960s onward. The specific claims — that the low-intensity zone is privileged for this adaptation, and that 45 minutes is a threshold rather than a convention — rest on mechanistic reasoning and small studies. Higher-intensity work also drives mitochondrial biogenesis, in some comparisons more per unit time. Rated moderate evidence and moderate certainty on exactly that basis, which is lower than the confidence with which the claim is usually stated.
attrs.measurement_gap: The user cannot measure this function directly. Anything the interface shows them here is a proxy, and it should say so.

attrs.dose: 3–4 sessions weekly of 30–45 minutes of continuous or interval swimming. For a competent swimmer, structured sets (for example 10 × 100 m with short rest) deliver a more reliable aerobic stimulus than unstructured lengths, because stroke fatigue otherwise silently drops the intensity.
attrs.effect_size_reasoning: Rated moderate rather than large, and the reason is technique rather than physiology. The frame should show that the effect size here is conditional on skill in a way that walking and cycling are not.
attrs.heart_rate_correction: Heart rate runs roughly 10–13 bpm lower in the water at equivalent effort because of horizontal posture, cooler water and the diving reflex. Zone targets calculated on land will make a swimmer think they are working easier than they are — perceived exertion is the better guide in the pool.
attrs.evidence_note: The swim-specific outcome literature is thinner and drawn from smaller samples than the running, walking and cycling literature. Rated moderate evidence for that reason, not because the physiology differs.
attrs.joint_advantage: Essentially no impact loading — the reason this is the default substitute when knee osteoarthritis, plantar fasciitis, stress reaction or low back pain block running or rucking.
attrs.bone_caveat: The flip side of zero impact: swimming contributes essentially nothing to bone density, and swimmers show lower bone mineral density than land-based athletes. Someone swimming because running is blocked needs a separate answer for bone.

attrs.dose: Roughly 1.6 g/kg/day is where the meta-analytic benefit for lean mass with resistance training plateaus. Distribute across 3–4 meals of 25–40 g rather than concentrating at dinner. The evidence supports going higher than the RDA. It does not currently demonstrate additional lean-mass benefit above roughly 1.6 g/kg, so the higher target is recorded as an author position rather than folded into the rating. Intakes at that level appear safe in normal kidney function, but safe is not the same as better.

attrs.evidence_quality: Among the strongest dietary edges in this graph — prospective cohorts and randomised trials both point the same way, with a dose-response, which is unusual in nutrition.
attrs.mechanism: Slows gastric emptying and carbohydrate absorption; the fermentable fraction produces short-chain fatty acids with additional metabolic signalling.

attrs.dose: 25–35 g/day sustained. Cereal fibre specifically carries the strongest cohort association with lower diabetes incidence.

attrs.dose: A sustained deficit producing 5–10 percent body weight loss over 3–6 months. Five percent already improves hepatic and adipose insulin sensitivity measurably; each further increment adds more, with no plateau found up to about 16 percent in graded studies.
attrs.why_adherence_is_rated_low: Regain is the modal outcome and is physiologically defended by falling energy expenditure and rising appetite signalling. This is a statement about biology, not willpower, and the frame should present it that way.
attrs.risk_note: Rated low rather than negligible: applied to someone without excess adiposity this becomes harmful, and rapid loss without adequate protein and resistance training costs lean mass.

attrs.dose: 3–5 percent weight loss reduces hepatic steatosis; 7–10 percent is the threshold associated with improvement in steatohepatitis; roughly 10 percent or more is where fibrosis regression starts appearing.
attrs.speed: Hepatic fat falls faster than almost anything else in this graph — substantial reductions are measurable on MRI-PDFF within two to four weeks, well before the scale moves much.
attrs.guideline_status: Weight loss is the first-line recommendation in the MASLD guideline, with these thresholds stated explicitly — one of the few places where an intervention and its dose-response are both formally endorsed.

attrs.dose: For prevention, 5–7 percent loss plus 150 minutes weekly of activity — the DPP protocol, which cut progression to diabetes by 58 percent. For remission in recent-onset type 2 diabetes, 15 kg or roughly 15 percent, as in DiRECT.
attrs.magnitude: The largest single effect in this entire graph. DPP outperformed metformin; DiRECT achieved remission in 46 percent at one year.
attrs.risk_note: Rated moderate because in someone taking insulin or a sulfonylurea, rapid improvement in glycaemic control without medication adjustment causes hypoglycaemia. That is a medication-supervision matter, and the modifier edges that encode it are owned elsewhere in the graph.

attrs.dose: A deficit of roughly 500 kcal/day, with protein held at 1.6 g/kg or above and resistance training maintained throughout. Without those two guardrails, a quarter or more of the weight lost is lean mass.
attrs.visceral_priority: Visceral fat falls preferentially early in a deficit, which means the metabolic benefit arrives ahead of the cosmetic one — worth telling people, because the mirror lags the bloodwork.
attrs.risk_note: Moderate: lean mass loss, and in older adults the accompanying bone loss, are real harms of unguarded weight loss.

attrs.dose: An 8–10 hour eating window, ideally ending in the early evening. Early windows outperform late ones on glycaemic measures in small crossover trials; late windows are what people actually manage.
attrs.honest_downgrade: Rated small and low deliberately, against the weight of enthusiasm this intervention carries in the longevity community. Its practical value is as a way of eating less without counting — which is a real benefit, but a different claim from the metabolic one usually made.

attrs.dose: 7–9 hours of sleep opportunity nightly. Experimental restriction to 4–5 hours reduced measured insulin sensitivity by a large margin within under a week in healthy young adults.

attrs.evidence_shape: Strong short-term experimental data plus consistent cohort associations; what is missing is a trial showing that extending habitually short sleep produces durable metabolic benefit, which is a much harder study to run.
attrs.effort_note: Rated moderate rather than trivial. For anyone with young children, shift work or insomnia, 'sleep more' is not a low-effort instruction, and treating it as free advice is a failure of realism.

citations: Whelton et al. 2017 ACC/AHA Hypertension Guideline
Ettehad et al. Lancet 2016
SPRINT MIND Investigators, JAMA 2019

attrs.reason: Rapidly absorbed liquid carbohydrate is the largest single contributor to glycaemic exposure in most diets that produce an elevated HbA1c, and removing it is a discrete, achievable change rather than a diffuse instruction to eat better.

citations: Malik & Hu, J Am Coll Cardiol 2015
Imamura et al. BMJ 2015
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2025

attrs.reason: An elevated HbA1c is a late signal — it moves only after years of compensatory hyperinsulinaemia. By the time it is abnormal, the process is well advanced and the case for acting is correspondingly stronger.
attrs.measurement_shift: Warrants adding a marker that can see the shape of a day, since a quarterly average cannot show which meals or which times are responsible.

citations: Tabák et al. Lancet 2009

attrs.baseline_incidence: roughly 2–10 injuries per 1000 hours of running in recreational runners, with novices at the high end of that range and up to a quarter to a third of new runners injured within their first year
attrs.severity_note: Mostly self-limiting overuse injury — tendinopathy, patellofemoral pain, shin pain. A minority (bone stress injury) requires months away from loading.
attrs.incidence_note: Risk concentrates in the first three months and in weeks where volume rises quickly. It is not evenly distributed across the year, so an annual average understates the early danger.
modifiers_that_raise_it: prior injury at the same site
attrs.why_it_is_authored: This is the single largest reason a running programme fails. Leaving it out of the comparison frame would make running look strictly better than swimming, which is not true.

citations: Videbæk et al. Sports Med 2015 — incidence of running-related injuries per 1000 hours
Nielsen et al. Int J Sports Phys Ther 2012 — training errors and running injury
van Gent et al. Br J Sports Med 2007 — injuries in long-distance runners

attrs.baseline_incidence: very low in absolute terms — on the order of one cardiac arrest per 100,000 to 200,000 hours of vigorous exertion in adults, and roughly one per 100,000 participants in long-distance running events
attrs.severity_note: Catastrophic when it happens, which is why it appears at all despite the tiny incidence.
attrs.incidence_note: Habitual exercise substantially lowers overall cardiac risk; the transient elevation during exertion is real and is greatest in people who are habitually sedentary and start abruptly. Zone 2 by definition is not vigorous for a trained person, so this edge applies mainly at initiation.
attrs.red_flag_note: Exertional chest pain or syncope is a clinician-routing matter, authored as a blocking modifier edge elsewhere in the graph.

citations: Franklin et al. Circulation 2020 — exercise-related acute cardiovascular events
Kim et al. NEJM 2012 — cardiac arrest during long-distance running races
Albert et al. NEJM 2000 — triggering of sudden death by vigorous exertion

attrs.baseline_incidence: uncommon in temperate conditions; rises steeply with heat and humidity, and event-day rates in hot races can reach several cases per 1000 participants
attrs.severity_note: Ranges from heat exhaustion, which resolves with rest and cooling, to exertional heat stroke, which is a medical emergency with meaningful mortality if cooling is delayed.
attrs.incidence_note: Humidity matters more than temperature because it is what blocks evaporative cooling. Acclimatisation over roughly 10–14 days substantially reduces risk.
attrs.note: Duration-heavy Zone 2 sessions carry more cumulative heat exposure than short hard sessions, so the long easy run is the one that gets people in the heat.

citations: Casa et al. J Athl Train 2015 — NATA position statement on exertional heat illnesses
Racinais et al. Br J Sports Med 2015 — consensus on training and competing in the heat

attrs.baseline_incidence: very low absolute risk, but the transient relative risk during vigorous exertion is elevated several-fold over rest and is highest in the habitually inactive
attrs.severity_note: Cardiac arrest or infarction. Rare and catastrophic.
attrs.incidence_note: This is the intervention in the graph where the transient risk is highest, because it is by design maximal-effort work. The correct response is graded entry after a base of easy volume, not avoidance — habitual vigorous exercisers have lower overall risk than the sedentary.
modifiers_that_raise_it: age over 50 starting intervals without a base

citations: Franklin et al. Circulation 2020
Albert et al. NEJM 2000
Fletcher et al. Circulation 2013

attrs.baseline_incidence: higher per hour than steady-state training at the same modality; interval sessions concentrate high tissue loading into a short window
attrs.severity_note: Acute muscle strains alongside the usual overuse pattern. Hamstring and calf strains are the characteristic injuries.
attrs.incidence_note: Total exposure hours are low, so the per-week absolute risk can still be modest. Adequate warm-up and limiting to one or two sessions weekly are the main mitigations.
modifiers_that_raise_it: more than two hard sessions weekly
running as the chosen interval modality rather than cycling or rowing

citations: Buchheit & Laursen, Sports Med 2013 — high-intensity interval training programming
Videbæk et al. Sports Med 2015
Weston et al. Br J Sports Med 2014

attrs.baseline_incidence: very low in supervised pools; substantially higher in open water, and higher again when swimming alone or after alcohol
attrs.severity_note: Fatal or causing hypoxic brain injury. Unlike every other adverse outcome attached to an aerobic intervention in this graph, there is no mild version worth planning around.
attrs.incidence_note: The absolute rate for a competent adult swimming lengths in a lifeguarded pool is very small. The rate is not small for open-water swimming alone, for weak swimmers, or where a cardiac or seizure event occurs in the water — the same event that would be survivable on land is often not survivable in water.
attrs.why_this_matters_for_ranking: Swimming has the lowest musculoskeletal risk of any aerobic modality and the only fatal tail risk. A single averaged risk band would hide both facts. The frame should show swimming as low-risk for injury and requiring a specific safety context — supervised water, competent stroke, never alone — rather than collapsing it to one word.

citations: WHO Global Report on Drowning 2014 and drowning fact sheet 2024
Szpilman et al. NEJM 2012 — drowning
Bierens et al. Br J Sports Med 2016 — drowning prevention in open water

attrs.baseline_incidence: low overall; shoulder pain is the characteristic complaint and affects a substantial minority of people who swim high weekly volume, particularly with freestyle-dominant training
attrs.severity_note: Almost entirely overuse shoulder pain — impingement-type symptoms that respond to volume reduction, stroke correction and scapular strengthening. Rarely disabling.
attrs.incidence_note: Per hour, the lowest musculoskeletal risk of any aerobic modality in this graph, which is precisely why swimming is the substitute of choice when lower-limb injury blocks running.

citations: Wanivenhaus et al. Sports Health 2012 — epidemiology of swimming injuries
Tanaka H. Int J Sports Med 2009
Gomez-Bruton et al. Sports Med 2013

attrs.baseline_incidence: low overuse injury rate per hour compared with running; the dominant risk outdoors is traumatic, from collisions and falls, and varies enormously with local road environment
attrs.severity_note: Overuse complaints are minor — knee pain from poor bike fit, neck and low back discomfort. Collision trauma is the severe tail and is a road-environment property, not a training-load one.
attrs.incidence_note: Indoor cycling removes the traumatic risk almost entirely, which is a meaningful and often overlooked reason to prefer it in a hostile traffic environment.

citations: Oja et al. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2011
de Rome et al. Accid Anal Prev 2014 — cycling injury patterns
Celis-Morales et al. BMJ 2017

attrs.baseline_incidence: clearly higher than unloaded walking; military load-carriage cohorts report substantial rates of foot blistering, low back pain, knee pain and stress injury, rising steeply with load mass, distance and rate of progression
attrs.severity_note: Mostly foot and soft-tissue problems and low back pain. Bone stress injury and rucksack palsy — a traction injury to the brachial plexus from shoulder straps — are the more serious tail.
attrs.incidence_note: Load, distance and speed multiply rather than add. The military literature is the best available source and comes from young populations under compulsion, so it likely understates risk in older recreational users progressing on their own.
modifiers_that_raise_it: load above roughly 20 percent of body weight
increasing load and distance in the same week

citations: Knapik et al. Mil Med 2004
Orr et al. Appl Ergon 2014 — load carriage injury risk factors
Roy et al. Mil Med 2010 — load carriage and musculoskeletal complaints

attrs.baseline_incidence: low back pain is the most common complaint in rowers, affecting a large minority over a season, with rib stress fractures a less common but characteristic injury
attrs.severity_note: Low back pain can be persistent and is the reason rowing is cautioned rather than recommended in anyone with an existing lumbar problem.
attrs.incidence_note: Strongly technique-dependent. Loaded lumbar flexion under fatigue is the mechanism, so risk rises sharply in long erg pieces performed with deteriorating form.
modifiers_that_raise_it: high stroke rate with heavy drag

citations: Thornton et al. Clin J Sport Med 2017 — rowing injury prevention consensus
Wilson et al. Br J Sports Med 2010 — low back pain in rowers
Yoshiga & Higuchi, Eur J Appl Physiol 2003

attrs.baseline_incidence: low per hour; ankle sprains and knee pain dominate, and the majority of hiking injuries occur on descent
attrs.severity_note: Usually minor. Consequence is amplified by remoteness — the same sprained ankle is trivial in a park and serious eight kilometres from a road.
attrs.incidence_note: Descent, fatigue late in a long day, and pack weight are the main drivers rather than total distance.

citations: Mitten et al. Am J Lifestyle Med 2018
Gatterer et al. Int J Environ Res Public Health 2021
Boulware et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003 — hiking injuries and illnesses

attrs.baseline_incidence: uncommon overall but a leading cause of search-and-rescue callouts in hot regions during summer months
attrs.severity_note: Heat exhaustion through to heat stroke. Remoteness and limited water carry make the trajectory worse than an equivalent episode near home.
attrs.incidence_note: Long duration at moderate intensity in sun with limited shade and finite water is the classic setup — arguably a higher heat exposure than a short hard run in the same conditions.

citations: Casa et al. J Athl Train 2015
Racinais et al. Br J Sports Med 2015
Boulware et al. Wilderness Environ Med 2003

attrs.baseline_incidence: essentially zero in people not taking insulin or insulin secretagogues; uncommon but real in those who are, particularly when the walk follows a mealtime insulin dose
attrs.severity_note: Usually mild and self-treated. Severe episodes are rare at this exercise intensity and duration.
attrs.incidence_note: The mechanism is the intervention working as intended — insulin-independent glucose uptake stacked on top of injected insulin. Included so that the graph does not present a universally trivial intervention as trivially safe for everyone.
modifiers_that_raise_it: longer or brisker walk than usual

citations: Riddell et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2017 — exercise management in insulin-treated diabetes
Colberg et al. Diabetes Care 2016
ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2025

attrs.baseline_incidence: negligible in people not on glucose-lowering medication; meaningful in those taking insulin or sulfonylureas, where an extended fast without dose adjustment is a recognised cause of hypoglycaemia
attrs.severity_note: Can be severe in insulin-treated people, particularly overnight or when the fast is extended beyond the planned window.
attrs.incidence_note: Entirely a medication-interaction risk rather than a property of fasting itself. Anyone on these agents needs the regimen reviewed before compressing their eating window, which is a clinician conversation and not something this graph resolves.
modifiers_that_raise_it: extending the fast beyond the intended window
unaccustomed exercise during the fasted period

Riddell et al. Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2017
Lowe et al. JAMA Intern Med 2020

attrs.baseline_incidence: negligible without glucose-lowering medication; common enough in insulin- or sulfonylurea-treated people that structured weight-loss programmes build medication de-escalation into the protocol from day one
attrs.severity_note: Can be severe. In DiRECT, medication withdrawal at the start of the intervention was a defining part of the design rather than an afterthought.
attrs.incidence_note: Improving insulin sensitivity rapidly while drug doses stay fixed is a predictable route to hypoglycaemia. Predictable means preventable, with supervision.
modifiers_that_raise_it: rapid or very low energy deficit
